title: Carnacki, the Ghost-Finder
author: William Hope Hodgson
written: 1910-12, for The Idler and The New Magazine
setting: A dining room at 427 Cheyne Walk, Chelsea, and whatever house Carnacki has just come back from — a Kentish manor, an Irish castle, a Galway billiard room, a Sussex chapel
lengthNote: Six cases, about 70,000 words, each told after dinner to the same four friends and each ending with the same two words
openingLine: In response to Carnacki's usual card of invitation to have dinner and listen to a story, I arrived promptly at 427, Cheyne Walk, to find the three others who were always invited to these happy little times, there before me.
summary: Carnacki investigates haunted houses the way a surveyor investigates subsidence: he measures the room, photographs it, seals the doors with tape, chalks a circle, and sits inside a ring of vacuum tubes he calls the Electric Pentacle. Some of the six cases turn out to be frauds and he says so; some are not, and the defences barely hold. The structure never varies — dinner, the story, and then Out you go! — and the repetition is the point, because it is the only thing in the book that can be relied on.
referenceStyle: story number and title, following the magazine texts

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Five cases ran in The Idler in 1910; The Thing Invisible followed in The New Magazine in 1912.

atAGlance.label: First collected
atAGlance.note: Eveleigh Nash published the six stories as a book; three more were added by Arkham House in 1947.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: A card of invitation, a dinner, a story told without interruption, and a dismissal.

atAGlance.label: The kit
atAGlance.note: The Electric Pentacle is Hodgson's own invention: an occult defence that needs a battery.

structure.label: The frame
structure.title: 427 Cheyne Walk, and four men who are told to leave
structure.summary: Every story is set inside the same evening: a card arrives, four friends dine, Carnacki refuses to be drawn until he is ready, tells the whole case without being interrupted, answers a question or two, and then throws them out. The narrator Dodgson records it. The frame gives the book its rhythm and its one joke.

scenes.title: The card
scenes.summary: The usual invitation to dinner and a story, and four men who never decline it.

scenes.title: Out you go
scenes.summary: The same genial dismissal closes each case, whatever has just been described.

structure.label: The apparatus
structure.title: Chalk, tape, garlic and a battery
structure.summary: Carnacki's procedure is the book's real subject: measure the room, photograph everything, seal the doors and windows with tape and wax so that no human agent can enter, then build the defences — a chalk circle, a water circle, bread and garlic, and the Electric Pentacle wired to accumulators. The reader learns the drill and then watches it be tested.

scenes.ref: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
scenes.title: The Electric Pentacle
scenes.summary: Hodgson's invention arrives in the first case: vacuum tubes laid in a pentacle and switched on.

scenes.ref: No. 2, The House Among the Laurels
scenes.title: Thirty-three feet
scenes.summary: A circle measured with a tape rule, men posted inside it, and their pipes confiscated because the Sigsand MS. forbids light within the barrier.

scenes.ref: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
scenes.title: The Sigsand MS.
scenes.summary: A fourteenth-century manuscript quoted in invented spelling, and treated as a technical reference rather than as a curiosity.

structure.label: Cases that are real
structure.title: The room, the ring and the hoof
structure.summary: In three of the six, something is genuinely there. A ring and a bed-chamber produce a hand that hunts; a room in Ireland swells and whistles like a mouth; and in Galway a hoof walks through a closed door and down a passage between two men. These are the stories the book is remembered for, and in each the defences are nearly not enough.

scenes.ref: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
scenes.title: The Grey Room
scenes.summary: A door that unlocks itself, a hand in the pentacle, and a ring that turns out to be the gateway.

scenes.title: The mouth
scenes.summary: A room in an Irish castle that whistles, and that Carnacki eventually sees as a vast pair of lips.

scenes.ref: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
scenes.title: The hoof in the passage
scenes.summary: The sound of a great hoof passing between two men in the dark, after a human fraud has already been exposed.

structure.label: Cases that are not
structure.title: Where the ghost is a man with a motive
structure.summary: Carnacki is as pleased to find a hoax as a haunting, and says so. A chapel dagger that stabs by itself turns out to be machinery and a butler; a house among the laurels has a human explanation running alongside the inhuman one; and a family curse is being helped along by somebody who wants a marriage stopped. The detections are fair and the clues are given.

scenes.title: The chapel dagger
scenes.summary: A weapon that strikes on its own, explained by mechanism, timing and a man with a reason.

scenes.ref: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
scenes.title: Two causes at once
scenes.summary: A human impostor is caught, and the hoof goes on sounding afterwards.

scenes.ref: No. 5, The Searcher of the End House
scenes.title: His mother's house
scenes.summary: The only case in his own home, with a smell, a child's footsteps and a long dull vigil that turns.

characters.name: Thomas Carnacki
characters.summary: A professional investigator who believes in neither ghosts nor the absence of them until he has measured the room. He is brusque about being questioned, exact about his equipment, and honest when a case collapses into fraud. What makes him unusual among occult detectives is that he is frightened, reports it, and goes back in anyway.
characters.clue: Seals a room with tape and wax, then sits inside a pentacle of vacuum tubes until something happens.
characters.firstAppearance: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster

characters.name: Dodgson
characters.role: The narrator, one of the four guests
characters.summary: He records the evenings and almost never intrudes. His one function is to be the man who asks a question too early in the first story and is politely frozen out, which teaches the reader the rules of the house.
characters.clue: Changes the subject to a new gun when he has asked one question too many.
characters.firstAppearance: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster

characters.name: Arkright
characters.role: The guest who asks the technical questions
characters.summary: He is the reason the reader learns anything about the theory: at the end of a case he asks what governs the Unknown Last Line of the Saaamaaa Ritual, and gets an answer about astral vibration and a protective force. Hodgson uses him to deliver exposition without slowing the stories.
characters.clue: Asks about the Unknown Last Line, and is told to read Harzan's Monograph.
characters.firstAppearance: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster

characters.name: The Sigsand MS.
characters.role: A fourteenth-century manuscript, quoted as a manual
characters.summary: Hodgson's invented authority, written in a spelling of his own devising and cited the way an engineer cites a standard. It supplies the rules — no light within the barrier, the five hills, the properties of the circle — and its flat practicality is what makes the occult in these stories feel like a trade.
characters.clue: Warns that there must be no light from within the barrier, in fourteenth-century spelling.
characters.firstAppearance: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster

characters.name: The Outer Monstrosities
characters.summary: Never described and barely named, they are the ab-human forces the pentacle keeps out. Hodgson gives them a theory rather than a shape: they press on the human from outside, and something inscrutable stands between them and the soul.
characters.clue: Their nearness produces a spiritual sickness worse than any physical pain.
characters.firstAppearance: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster

themes.name: Sealing the room first
themes.summary: Before anything supernatural is entertained, Carnacki eliminates people: tape across the doors, wax on the windows, photographs of every wall. The haunting only begins once fraud has been ruled out in front of the reader.
themes.development: The method is set out in the first case, tested in the middle ones, and in the last it catches a hoax instead of a ghost — which is the proof that the method was never rigged.

themes.name: An occult trade with a literature
themes.summary: The stories assume a profession: manuscripts to consult, monographs to read, rituals with numbered signs, and defences that can be built wrong. Carnacki's authority comes from reading, not from a gift.
themes.development: Each case adds a scrap of the system — the Saaamaaa Ritual, the Unknown Last Line, the Incantation of Raaaee — and none of it is ever explained fully enough to be checked.

themes.name: A defence that needs a battery
themes.summary: The Electric Pentacle is the book's best idea: the mediaeval figure of protection, wired with vacuum tubes and run off accumulators. Edwardian electricity meets a fourteenth-century manuscript and neither is treated as absurd.
themes.development: It is introduced as an improvement, relied on in every serious case, and its weakness — it can be broken by a hand reaching across it — is what makes the first story frightening.

themes.name: The evening as a ritual
themes.summary: The card, the dinner, the refusal to be hurried, the story told without interruption, the dismissal. The frame is as fixed as the pentacle, and it does the same job: it holds a shape around something unruly.
themes.development: Six stories, one unvarying evening, and the reader comes to want the closing words as much as the guests do.

themes.name: Something on our side
themes.summary: The one piece of comfort in Hodgson's universe is stated in an aside: an inscrutable protective force intervenes between the human soul and what is outside. It is not called God and it does not always arrive early.
themes.development: It saves Carnacki in the first case, is discussed as theory in the fourth, and is never claimed as certain.

themes.name: An investigator who admits it
themes.summary: Carnacki reports his own terror as part of the evidence: the sweat, the cowed feeling, the spiritual sickness that comes with the ab-human. In a genre of unflappable experts, that is the collection's most modern quality.
themes.development: He is frightened in the first story and still frightened in the sixth, and never pretends the experience gets easier.

techniques.name: The club tale
techniques.definition: A story told aloud to a fixed audience inside another story.
techniques.inThisBook: The dinner at Cheyne Walk supplies the audience, the interruptions and the closing question. It also lets Hodgson end a case without resolving it: a man telling a story after dinner is allowed to say he never found out.

techniques.name: Out you go
techniques.definition: A phrase repeated at the same point in every story.
techniques.inThisBook: Carnacki's dismissal closes all six cases. Coming after a hand in the dark or a hoof in the passage, it works as the door of the barrier closing — the evening is sealed and everyone goes home.

techniques.name: Equipment as plot
techniques.definition: A story advanced by the state of its tools.
techniques.inThisBook: Chalk, tape, wax, garlic, a camera, a tape measure and a battery. Whether a case ends well depends on whether the circle is complete and the tubes are lit, which gives the supernatural something to break.

techniques.name: A single witness, telling it afterwards
techniques.definition: An account with no corroboration beyond the teller.
techniques.inThisBook: Carnacki's photographs are described but not shown, and his friends never visit the houses. The frame makes the whole book one man's word, which the fraud cases then quietly reinforce: he is the sort who would say so if it were a trick.

techniques.name: Old houses, handled professionally
techniques.definition: The haunted-house tradition approached as a job of work.
techniques.inThisBook: The manor, the castle and the chapel are all conventional, and everything Carnacki does in them is not. The contrast between inherited dread and a man with a tape measure is the collection's whole comic and dramatic engine.

techniques.name: The Sigsand spelling
techniques.definition: Invented archaic orthography used for quoted authority.
techniques.inThisBook: Theyre must noe lyght come from wythin the barryier. The spelling is fake and the effect is not: it turns the rules into something older than the man obeying them.

quotations.text: In response to Carnacki's usual card of invitation to have dinner and listen to a story, I arrived promptly at 427, Cheyne Walk
quotations.reference: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
quotations.context: The first sentence of the collection, and of five of the six stories.
quotations.analysis: The word usual is doing the work: before we have met anyone we know this has happened many times and will happen again. Hodgson establishes a routine so that the things inside it can be as irregular as he likes.

quotations.context: Carnacki's dismissal, which ends each case.
quotations.analysis: Three words, genially delivered, immediately after something that ought to keep four grown men talking all night. The formula is a door closing on the subject, and by the third story the reader is waiting for it.

quotations.text: the Electric Pentacle, which is a most marvelous 'Defense'
quotations.reference: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
quotations.context: Introducing his own improvement on the traditional protective circle.
quotations.analysis: Hodgson's single best invention, and the reason these stories still feel unlike anything else: a mediaeval figure of protection rewired with vacuum tubes. The quotation marks around Defense are Carnacki's, and they are the mark of a man using a technical term from an old book.

quotations.text: Theyre must noe lyght come from wythin the barryier.
quotations.reference: No. 2, The House Among the Laurels
quotations.context: Quoted from the Sigsand MS. as he takes the men's pipes away.
quotations.analysis: An invented fourteenth-century sentence used as a safety regulation. The spelling makes it old, the context makes it operational, and the pipes being confiscated makes it real.

quotations.text: I got my tape measure then, and measured out a circle thirty-three feet
quotations.reference: No. 2, The House Among the Laurels
quotations.context: Setting the defences in the great hall.
quotations.analysis: A tape measure, in a haunted house, stated without irony. The whole method is in this clause: the occult is being handled by somebody who would rather be precise than impressive.

quotations.text: this was no piece of silly mumming on my part; but done with a definite intention of erecting a barrier
quotations.reference: No. 2, The House Among the Laurels
quotations.context: Warning the men who will spend the night inside the circle.
quotations.analysis: He anticipates the reader's scepticism and answers it in the tone of a foreman explaining a safety rule. Hodgson keeps making the characters take the ritual seriously as procedure, which is the only way the ritual can frighten anyone.

quotations.text: that feeling of spiritual sickness, as if some delicate, beautiful, inward grace had suffered, which is felt only upon the too near approach of the ab-human
quotations.reference: No. 1, The Gateway of the Monster
quotations.context: In the pentacle, as the thing in the Grey Room comes close.
quotations.analysis: The damage is moral rather than physical, and Carnacki says it is worse than pain. This is the sentence that separates Hodgson's monsters from the period's ghosts: what they threaten is not the body but something the narrator can only call grace.

quotations.text: the sound of a hoof in the dark billiard room we had just left
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: Just after the rational explanation has begun to look convincing.
quotations.analysis: Hodgson's timing is exact: the noise arrives in the sentence immediately after Carnacki has started listing commonplace possibilities. The detective story is allowed to nearly succeed before the ghost story takes it back.

quotations.text: The clungk clunck, clungk clunck, of the great hoof falls passed right between us
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: Two men flattened against opposite walls of a passage.
quotations.analysis: An invented noise, repeated, with no creature attached to it. The onomatopoeia is faintly ridiculous on the page and works completely in the ear, which is the risk Hodgson takes throughout and usually wins.

quotations.text: the shape of a single enormous hoof
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: In a photograph taken during the haunting, examined afterwards.
quotations.analysis: The evidence is photographic, which for 1910 is the most modern proof available, and it still shows only a shape half-formed out of shadow. Carnacki studies it for a long time without understanding it better, and says so.

quotations.text: there is some inscrutable Protective Force constantly intervening between the human soul
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: Answering Arkright's question about what governs the Unknown Last Line.
quotations.analysis: The nearest thing to consolation in Hodgson, and it arrives as jargon at the end of a story rather than as revelation. Inscrutable is the operative word: something is on our side and nobody knows what it is.

quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.context: In the same explanation, naming what the protective force stands between us and.
quotations.analysis: Capitalised, plural, and never described. Hodgson's habit of naming forces he will not show gave later writers a whole vocabulary, and the restraint is why the phrase still carries weight.

quotations.text: the Unknown Last Line of the Saaamaaa Ritual
quotations.reference: No. 4, The Horse of the Invisible
quotations.analysis: A named thing that is defined as unknown, in a ritual with numbered signs and a missing eighth place. The apparatus is elaborate enough to sound like scholarship and vague enough that nothing can be checked — exactly the balance the stories need.

timeline.label: Hodgson born in Essex
timeline.detail: A clergyman's son, and the second of twelve children.

timeline.label: Hodgson apprenticed to the sea
timeline.detail: Eight years afloat, including a Royal Humane Society medal for a rescue in heavy weather.

timeline.label: Hodgson opens a gymnasium in Blackburn
timeline.detail: He left the sea for physical culture, photography and lecturing; the practical streak in Carnacki comes from here.

timeline.label: Hodgson's first novel, The Boats of the Glen Carrig
timeline.detail: The Boats of the Glen Carrig, then The House on the Borderland the following year.

timeline.label: First five stories published in The Idler
timeline.detail: The Gateway of the Monster, The House Among the Laurels, The Whistling Room, The Horse of the Invisible and The Searcher of the End House.

timeline.label: The Thing Invisible published in The New Magazine
timeline.detail: The sixth case appears in The New Magazine, and is the most detective-like of them.

timeline.label: First book edition, published by Eveleigh Nash
timeline.detail: The six stories are published as a book.

timeline.label: Hodgson killed at Ypres
timeline.detail: A shell killed him in April, aged forty; he had re-enlisted after being invalided out.

timeline.label: Arkham House edition adds three more cases
timeline.detail: The Haunted Jarvee, The Find and The Hog are printed from manuscripts; later editions often run to nine cases.

places.name: Cheyne Walk, Chelsea
places.note: Carnacki's address, where every story is told over dinner.

places.name: County Galway
places.note: The country of the Horse of the Invisible, and of the Irish castle in The Whistling Room.

places.name: Kent
places.note: The manor country of the earlier cases, close enough to London for a night train.

places.name: Blackburn, Lancashire
places.note: Where Hodgson taught physical culture and began photographing storms.

places.name: Borth, Ceredigion
places.note: The Welsh coast where he was living when the Carnacki stories were written.

criticalViews.summary: Carnacki investigates with equipment, photographs and a documented method, and every later ghost-hunter with a kit bag descends from him.
criticalViews.counter: Le Fanu's Hesselius and Blackwood's John Silence came earlier; what is new in Hodgson is not the detective but the hardware.

criticalViews.position: The frauds make the hauntings credible
criticalViews.summary: Because two of the six cases are exposed as human contrivance, the reader trusts Carnacki when he says the others were not.
criticalViews.counter: The exposures are also where the collection is weakest as fiction: the mechanical solutions are thin, and the stories everyone remembers are the ones with no explanation at all.

criticalViews.position: A formula worn out in six goes
criticalViews.summary: The invitation, the dinner, the uninterrupted narrative and the dismissal repeat exactly, and the later stories lean on the apparatus rather than developing it.
criticalViews.counter: The repetition is the form, as it is in any club tale. It is also the only stable thing in a universe Hodgson has already shown, in his novels, running down to nothing.

essayQuestions.question: What does Carnacki's method contribute to the horror?
essayQuestions.focus: Procedure, evidence and the value of ruling things out
plan: Set out the drill: photographs, tape and wax on the openings, chalk and water circles, the Electric Pentacle.
Show how eliminating human agency in front of the reader raises the cost of what is left.
Use The Thing Invisible, where the method catches a hoax, as the guarantee that it is not rigged.
Take the first story's broken circle as the moment the apparatus fails.
Argue for whether the equipment makes the stories more frightening or more comfortable.

essayQuestions.question: How does the club-tale frame shape what these stories can do?
essayQuestions.focus: Telling, audience and the unfinished case
plan: Describe the evening and its fixed order, including the dismissal.
Note what the frame permits: no corroboration, no visit to the house, and endings without answers.
Examine Arkright's questions as the only route to the theory behind the practice.
Compare the effect with a story told directly, in the moment.
Conclude on the repetition, and whether it reassures or confines.

essayQuestions.question: Why does the Electric Pentacle work as an idea?
plan: Describe the object: a mediaeval figure of protection, laid in vacuum tubes and run from accumulators.
Set it beside the Sigsand MS., with its invented fourteenth-century spelling.
Consider what Edwardian readers knew of electricity, and why that makes the join convincing.
Use the moment a hand crosses the tubes to show the device's dramatic value.
Argue for what later writers took from the combination.

discussionQuestions: Carnacki admits to being frightened in almost every case. Does that make him more or less reliable?
Two of the six turn out to be frauds. Would the book be better if all six were real?
The Sigsand MS. is invented, and quoted as though it were not. Why does that work?
What is gained by never describing the Outer Monstrosities?
Every story ends with the same two words. What do they do to the horror that came before them?
The photographs are described and never shown. Would you want to see them?

related.why: Hodgson's own novel of a besieged house, with the same practicality and none of the reassurance.
The method Carnacki is borrowing: a specialist, a client, an examination and an explanation over dinner.
A haunting with one witness and no corroboration, written fifteen years earlier and never resolved.
The other Edwardian-adjacent book where men fight the supernatural with equipment, timetables and written records.
Blackwood in the same years, doing without any apparatus at all.
